Reading a value walks from the requested version back to the root, taking time proportional to the distance from the root.

title: Move the root to the version you read most
takeaway: Rerooting turns repeated O(n) reads into O(1) reads by paying the path cost once.
section: Optimizing successive reads on the same version

blocks.text: The initial array has no claim to stay the root, so the tree can be rerooted at any version, with that node's cache array becoming the true copy of the array. Rerooting is a sequence of rotations along the path from the old root to the new one, costing time proportional to that distance and updating every node on the path. After rerooting, reads at that version are O(1), so the cost can be charged to reads or to updates depending on whether the workload is read-heavy or write-heavy.

title: Classify persistence by what edits each version allows
takeaway: Partial, full and confluent persistence differ in whether old versions can be written and whether versions can be merged.

blocks.text: A partially persistent structure lets every historical version be read but allows writes only to the newest one, so old versions behave as immutable snapshots. A fully persistent structure allows writes to any version, forking a new branch from history. A confluently persistent structure also allows two versions to be merged into a new one, which is what version-control-style branching and merging requires.

title: Path copying shares every node off the modified path
takeaway: Copying only the root-to-target path preserves the rest of the structure by reference, so an update costs depth rather than size.

blocks.text: Instead of deep-copying the whole structure on each write, path copying duplicates the nodes on the path from the root to the modified node and leaves every untouched subtree shared with the previous version. The new version gets a new root that points into the old structure everywhere except along that path, so memory and time per update scale with the depth of the node. This is why path copying suits linked structures such as lists and trees.

title: Constant folding pays for deterministic work once, at compile time
takeaway: Replacing a constant expression with its value removes runtime work and shrinks the bytecode.

blocks.text: `24 * 60 * 60` is folded to `86400` while the AST is built, so the bytecode contains a single `LOAD_CONST` instead of two multiplications. The optimizer does not fold everything: `2 ** 64` is folded but `4 ** 64` is not, and string expressions are folded only up to length 4096. Those limits mean a constant expression is not proof that folding happened, so check the disassembly rather than assuming.

title: Reuse the runtime operator inside the optimizer
takeaway: Calling the same evaluation function the interpreter uses keeps folded values semantically identical and avoids duplicate logic.

blocks.text: CPython's `fold_binop` inspects the operator and calls the ordinary numeric function, such as `PyNumber_Add` for addition, rather than implementing a separate constant-only evaluator. The folded result therefore comes from the same code path a runtime addition would use, so edge cases and type behavior cannot drift between the two. This removes the need for special-case folding functions for each pattern or type.

title: Interning makes equal strings the same pointer
takeaway: One canonical copy per value turns O(n) character comparison into a single pointer check and removes duplicate string objects.

blocks.text: An interned string is stored once, and every reference to that value points at the same object, so equality can be tested by comparing references instead of scanning characters. CPython's `interned` dictionary holds these canonical objects with each key mapped to the same object as its value, and the `PyUnicode_CHECK_INTERNED` macro reads a flag recording whether a string was interned. The same sharing follows the flyweight pattern and cuts memory when many identical strings appear.

title: Interning is partial, so never test string equality with `is`
takeaway: Compile-time literals get interned but runtime-built strings do not, so identity checks give correct answers only by accident.

blocks.text: CPython interns compile-time constants, names, string literals, dictionary keys and attribute names, but strings built during interpretation are not interned automatically. It also restricts literal interning to names matching `[a-zA-Z0-9_]*`, close to Python identifiers. Two equal strings can therefore be distinct objects, which makes `is` an unreliable equality test; use `==` unless identity is what you mean.

title: A decorator can trace recursion depth without editing the function
takeaway: Wrapping a recursive function lets you log entry and exit at the right indentation while leaving the algorithm untouched.

blocks.text: The decorator keeps a `recursion_level` counter, increments it before calling the wrapped function, and decrements it after the call returns, using the current value to indent each printed line. Printing a right arrow on entry and a left arrow with the return value on exit reconstructs the call tree in execution order. Applied to `fib(3)`, the trace shows both the descent into subproblems and the values bubbling back up.

reference.title: Easy tracing of nested function calls in Python

title: The rightmost set bit position estimates how many distinct values you have seen
takeaway: A bit vector of observed lowest-set-bit positions approximates cardinality with O(log m) space instead of storing every value.

blocks.text: For uniformly distributed hashes, the probability that the rightmost set bit sits at position k is 2^-(k+1), so observing position b implies roughly 2^b distinct values. Hash each stream element into a wide uniform range, set the bit for its rightmost set position, and take 2^b where b is the rightmost zero left in the vector. The raw estimate has a large error margin, which the original algorithm reduces by averaging across multiple hash functions and dividing by the correction factor 0.77351.

reference.title: Probabilistic Counting Algorithms for Data Base Applications

title: Duplicates do not change a bit-pattern sketch
takeaway: Because the sketch records which bit positions occurred rather than how often, repeated elements cost nothing and do not distort the estimate.

blocks.text: Flajolet-Martin observes only the rightmost set bit of each hashed element and sets that position in a bit vector, so an element appearing a million times sets the same bit once. The estimate depends on which positions were seen, not on stream length or frequency, which is why a single pass suffices. This is also why the approximation stays the same whether elements appear a million times or just a few times.

title: Admit a page to the main cache only after a second reference
takeaway: A probationary FIFO buffer between the miss and the LRU cache keeps one-off scans from flushing the working set.

blocks.text: A new faulted page enters a secondary FIFO buffer, `A1`, and only if it is referenced again does it move into the primary LRU buffer, `Am`. Pages from a table larger than the cache are touched once, so they age out of `A1` instead of evicting warmer pages from `Am`, which is exactly the loss LRU suffers on large scans. The cost is a tuning problem: too small an `A1` makes the hotness test too strict, while too large an `A1` shrinks `Am`.

reference.title: 2Q: A low overhead high-performance buffer management replacement algorithm

title: Keep evicted probationers' references to detect returning pages
takeaway: Remembering recently evicted cold pages lets a returning page skip probation and enter the hot cache directly.

blocks.text: Pages often get a burst of references and then go quiet, so 2Q splits the secondary buffer into `A1-In` for pages still in memory and `A1-Out` for references to pages already evicted. A page whose reference is found in `A1-Out` has come back after a gap, so it is promoted straight to `Am`. This removes most of the hand-tuning of the simplified two-buffer version without losing performance.

title: Let an element join the group of a friend already in the queue
takeaway: Grouping similar work at enqueue time amortizes setup costs by processing batches together.

blocks.text: Instead of assigning each element an explicit priority, an Israeli Queue enqueues an element at the tail of the group its friend belongs to, so related tasks stay contiguous, while an element with no friend starts a new group at the back. This pays off when setup is expensive relative to processing, such as downloading large metafiles, spinning up infrastructure, or establishing persistent connections, because a batch shares one setup. The original design processes a whole group in one go, which is the point when per-task time is much smaller than setup time.

title: Grouping beats fairness only while arrivals stay bounded
takeaway: Friend-based insertion invites starvation for elements with no friends if grouped arrivals keep cutting ahead.

blocks.text: Every insertion into an existing group jumps ahead of the elements queued behind that group, so a steady stream of friend-bearing arrivals can leave the rear of the queue waiting indefinitely. The structure therefore fits batchable, setup-heavy workloads, not latency-sensitive queues that promise bounded waiting. Processing a whole group per turn reduces how often the front of the queue is revisited but does not by itself remove the starvation risk.

title: Layer noise at several frequencies instead of generating each point randomly
takeaway: Summing weighted octaves produces natural-looking detail that neither pure randomness nor a single smoothed curve can.

blocks.text: Independent random heights at every point produce spikes and abrupt jumps that do not resemble real terrain. Generate several terrains with different sampling densities, then take a normalized weighted sum: the sparsest layer carries the broad smooth shape, while the densest layer contributes the small aberrations. With six layers, sampled points halve and weights double from 0.03125 to 1, so the fine detail never dominates the overall contour.

title: Interpolation turns a few sampled points into a smooth continuous curve
takeaway: Choosing an interpolation kernel is choosing how much sharpness to trade for smoothness.

blocks.text: Linear interpolation assumes intermediate points lie on the line between two known anchors, giving continuity but still angular transitions. Cosine interpolation places those points on a cosine curve through the anchors, removing the visible kinks and producing a curvier result. Sampling every k-th point of a naive random terrain and interpolating the rest removes spikes while keeping the sampled points as peaks.

title: MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity as the chance two sets share a minimum
takeaway: A sketch is useful when a random projection makes a cheap event occur with exactly the probability you need to estimate.

blocks.text: Under a random permutation of the universal set, the probability that two sets produce the same minimum element equals their Jaccard similarity, because that event happens exactly when the shared minimum lies in the intersection. MinHash stores k such minima per set, called a signature, and estimates similarity as the fraction of matching positions. Comparing k-item signatures replaces union and intersection over millions of documents with a few short comparisons.

title: Signature length is the accuracy dial for an approximate similarity score
takeaway: Approximation is acceptable at scale only when its error is understood and tunable.

blocks.text: A MinHash signature of k values gives an estimate whose error shrinks as k grows, so memory budget sets accuracy. Raw Jaccard comparison across every pair of millions of documents would take years, while signatures yield a good estimate with far fewer computations. Raise k when near-duplicates must be caught reliably and lower it when throughput matters more.

title: Smoothing window size trades noise removal against anomaly visibility
takeaway: Any smoothing parameter small enough to preserve anomalies is also small enough to leave noise behind.

blocks.text: A moving average with a short window leaves short-term irregularities intact, while a long window flattens the plot and hides the spikes being monitored. Aggregation is worse than smoothing here because it also reduces data density and can hide an anomaly outright. Choose the window against the monitoring goal rather than for the prettiest chart.

title: Choose the smoothing window that maximizes kurtosis
takeaway: Anomalies live in the tails, so the window that leaves the distribution heaviest-tailed is the one that keeps them visible.

blocks.text: Kurtosis measures the tailedness of a distribution, and adding even a small anomaly to a tail raises it sharply. Compute kurtosis of the smoothed series for each candidate window and pick the window that maximizes it, which strips short-term noise while preserving extreme values. Search within a bounded range such as 10 to 40 rather than globally, because the global maximum can distort the plot and lose information.

title: Bucket items by access count to make LFU updates constant time
takeaway: If a heap must reorder on every access, replace the ordering with buckets you can splice into.

blocks.text: A min-heap LFU cache rebalances on every insert, access, and eviction, making all three operations O(log n) even though finding the minimum is cheap. Instead keep a sorted list of frequency nodes, each owning a doubly linked list of values at that frequency, plus a hash table from key to value node. An access moves a node to the next frequency bucket through pointer changes alone, so all operations become O(1).

reference.title: An O(1) algorithm for implementing the LFU cache eviction scheme

title: Constant-time reads and updates are paid for in memory
takeaway: Optimizing read and update latency usually means spending memory instead.

blocks.text: The O(1) LFU design needs a hash table plus per-frequency and per-value doubly linked lists with back-pointers, all resident so pointer manipulation stays direct. The RUM conjecture frames this as a three-way tension: read, update, and memory overhead cannot all be minimized at once. Accept the extra pointers and allocations when cache latency dominates, and a simpler O(log n) policy when memory is the binding constraint.

title: Increment an approximate counter with probability set by the estimate gap
takeaway: A probabilistic increment rule can keep the expected estimate unbiased while cutting storage dramatically.

blocks.text: Morris stores v proportional to log(n), so after one more event the estimate should move from n to n+1. The gap between the event counts represented by v and v+1 gives d, the reciprocal of that jump, and v increments only when a uniform random draw falls below d. As n grows the gap widens, d shrinks, and increments become rarer, keeping the expected value at n+1 while the register holds only log(n).

reference.title: Counting large number of events in small registers

title: Logarithmic storage keeps relative error constant as counts grow
takeaway: Absolute error is the wrong target for a counter; constant relative error is what makes an approximate count usable at any scale.

blocks.text: Counting every other event with a coin flip doubles capacity but leaves relative error high for small counts and varying with n. Storing log(n) instead makes the register grow quickly at small n and slowly at large n, so relative error stays near constant no matter how many events arrive. Storing the logarithm is why counting to n needs only O(log log n) bits.

title: Recursion that multiplies overlapping subproblems is procrastination
takeaway: Splitting a problem is not the same as making it smaller; check whether the subproblems overlap before calling it divide and conquer.

blocks.text: Multiply and Surrender splits a problem into slightly simpler subproblems, multiplies them, and delays evaluation until solving can no longer be postponed. Naive recursive Fibonacci fits this shape: it branches into two calls with no memoization, repeating work and running in non-polynomial time while looking structurally like divide and conquer. The tell is identical subproblems appearing again and again, with a recurrence that grows faster than the work shrinks.

title: A deterministic slow algorithm beats a random one that can undo progress
takeaway: Worst-case time is not the only measure; guaranteed progress and convergence matter when correctness must hold.

blocks.text: Bogosort reshuffles until sorted, so one iteration can carry a nearly sorted array far away and the worst case is unbounded. Slowsort runs in O(n^log n) at best and never makes a wrong move: its inversion count is non-increasing, so each step leaves items correctly ordered relative to each other. Where progress must be monotonic, predictable slowness is safer than a gamble.

title: Put the index in memory and keep the data in an append-only log
takeaway: A hash index plus append-only files turns every write into a sequential write and every read into one seek.

blocks.text: Bitcask appends each key-value entry to an active datafile and records key to file and offset in an in-memory hash table called KeyDir. A write needs no disk seek, and a read needs one hash lookup plus one disk read at the recorded offset. The price is that the entire keyspace must fit in RAM, so shard keys across instances when it does not.

title: Treat updates and deletes as appends, then reclaim space by merging live records
takeaway: Append-only stores stay fast by never rewriting in place, and stay small by compacting later.

blocks.text: An update appends a new entry and repoints the index, and a delete appends a tombstone, leaving the old records dangling. A merge pass walks the immutable files and writes only the latest live value for each key into new datafiles, ignoring keys that no longer exist. Because merged records sit at new offsets, their KeyDir entries must be updated atomically as part of the same operation.

title: Output a continuous suspicion level instead of a binary up/down
takeaway: A boolean failure detector throws away the confidence that lets callers choose their own risk.

blocks.text: Phi accrual computes φ as the negative base-10 logarithm of the probability that the next heartbeat arrives later than t, so φ rises smoothly as the wait lengthens and tends to infinity if the process truly dies. On this scale a threshold of φ=1 means roughly a 10% chance of being contradicted by a late heartbeat, φ=2 about 1%, and φ=3 about 0.1%. Applications can therefore pick the threshold that matches their quality-of-service requirement instead of accepting one fixed verdict.

title: Derive the timeout from observed heartbeat intervals, not a fixed constant
takeaway: An adaptive detector learns each link's normal latency instead of forcing one timeout on every link.

blocks.text: A fixed timeout must be short enough to detect failure quickly and long enough to avoid false positives, and no single value satisfies both across variable networks. Phi accrual keeps a sliding window of recent heartbeat arrival times, derives the mean and variance of the intervals, and treats intervals as normally distributed. It then integrates the probability density beyond the current wait to estimate the probability that a heartbeat is merely late.

title: Compare ciphertext positions that share the same key byte to cancel it
takeaway: In a repeating-key cipher, the key length is the period at which differences between ciphertext bytes reveal differences between plaintext bytes.

blocks.text: XORing two ciphertext bytes encrypted with the same key byte yields the XOR of the corresponding plaintext bytes, because the key cancels: c[i] XOR c[j] equals p[i] XOR p[j]. Chunk the ciphertext at candidate lengths and average the normalized Hamming distance between chunks; the score drops sharply when the length is the key length or a multiple of it, since only then do positions align on the same key byte. That minimum identifies the key length before any brute force begins.

title: Normalize a distance before comparing streams of different lengths
takeaway: Raw Hamming distance rewards short comparisons; divide by bits compared to make scores comparable.

blocks.text: Hamming distance counts differing bits, so a longer pair of streams accumulates more differences regardless of how similar the streams are per byte. Hamming score divides that distance by the number of bit pairs compared. Normalized this way, random bytes average about 0.4999 while lowercase English letters average about 0.3072, which is what makes a low score meaningful evidence of aligned plaintext.

title: When the key space is small, enumerate every key and rank the results
takeaway: Brute force is the right attack when the secret space is small enough to exhaust.

blocks.text: A single-byte XOR cipher has only 256 possible keys, so decryption can be attempted with every value in [0, 256) instead of attacking the algorithm itself. Each attempt yields a candidate plaintext, and the candidates are ranked rather than inspected one by one. The same approach applies to any scheme whose secret space can be enumerated cheaply.

title: Score candidates by distance from a known frequency distribution
takeaway: A numeric distance to a reference distribution lets a program rank outputs that a human would judge by eye.

blocks.text: A Fitting Quotient compares a candidate text's letter frequencies with English letter frequencies by averaging the absolute differences between them, so a lower value means the text looks more like English. In the 256-key search, the key whose decryption minimizes the quotient is returned as the plaintext. The score becomes unreliable for very short texts or texts full of symbols, where the frequency profile is too noisy to separate candidates.

title: Iterability is a slot on the type, not a property of the value
takeaway: Protocol support is a per-type decision, so extending a primitive is a matter of filling one slot.

blocks.text: CPython represents every type as a PyTypeObject whose function-pointer slots implement pieces of behaviour, and the tp_iter slot holds the function behind `__iter__`. Integers are not iterable because `PyLong_Type` leaves `tp_iter` NULL; assigning a function that returns a range iterator makes every integer iterable at once. The function receives the integer and returns an iterator over `[0, n)` with step 1, so `for x in 7` behaves like `for x in range(0, 7, 1)`.

title: Adding a protocol to a primitive changes every context that uses it
takeaway: A type-level change reaches far beyond the syntax you intended to enable.
section: Why it is not a good idea

blocks.text: Unpacking iterates its right-hand side, so once integers are iterable, `a, b = 7` produces seven values for two targets and raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`, while `a, b = 2` succeeds. Two nearly identical statements therefore behave completely differently. Making a core type iterable silently changes assignment, loops, and every other construct that consumes the iterator protocol.

title: Cast a child struct to its parent only if the parent is its first member
takeaway: Prefix layout is what makes an upcast safe in a language without inheritance.

blocks.text: C allocates struct members contiguously in declaration order with no metadata, so a struct whose first member is a `list_head` has that member at offset zero. Casting `list_int *` to `list_head *` maps the parent's 8 bytes onto the first 8 bytes of the child, which are exactly the embedded `list_head`. The cast is only valid because of that prefix guarantee; a parent placed anywhere else in the child would not line up.

title: Write shared logic against the embedded parent, not each child type
takeaway: One function over the common prefix replaces a copy per variant.

blocks.text: List operations such as adding or deleting a node only manipulate `next` and `prev`, so they can accept `list_head *` and work for nodes holding integers, strings, or anything else. Python applies the same idea with `PyObject`, which holds the reference count and type and is embedded as the first member of every object, letting one reference-counting function serve all types. The parent struct carries the shared behaviour; each child struct only adds its own fields.

title: A storage design can optimize two of reads, updates, and memory
takeaway: Every access-method choice spends one of three budgets, so name the one you are giving up.

blocks.text: The RUM conjecture holds that no access method can be simultaneously optimal on read overhead, update cost, and space overhead; improving two tends to worsen the third. Read-optimized structures like B-trees and hash indexes keep auxiliary data that must be maintained on every write, while update-optimized LSM trees buffer deltas and pay in read and space overhead. The tradeoff is a conjecture rather than a theorem, but it gives a vocabulary for comparing storage engines against a workload.

reference.title: Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture

title: Measure storage overheads as amplification ratios against the main data
takeaway: Amplification ratios make read, write, and space costs comparable across designs.

blocks.text: Read amplification is the total data read, main plus auxiliary, divided by the main data actually requested; write amplification applies the same ratio to writes; space amplification compares total space used with the space of the main data alone. A secondary index consulted on every read raises read amplification, and the writes needed to keep it current raise write amplification. Expressing overheads this way turns a vague claim that a structure is fast into a number tied to a specific workload.

title: Hashing modulo the node count remaps almost every key when nodes change
takeaway: A mapping tied to the cluster size turns scaling into a full data migration.

blocks.text: With five storage nodes, a file's home is `hash(path) mod 5`; adding two nodes changes the modulus to 7 and reassigns nearly every file. In the worked example, all five files move to different nodes after the scale-up. Even moving half the data on each resize is too expensive to sustain, which is the problem consistent hashing exists to remove.

title: Place keys and nodes on one fixed ring and assign each key to the next node
takeaway: Making the hash space constant and huge keeps key-to-node mappings stable as the cluster changes.

blocks.text: Both objects and storage nodes hash into a fixed space such as `[0, 2^128 - 1]`, and an object belongs to the first node clockwise from its position, wrapping at the end. The hash function no longer depends on how many nodes exist, so adding a node only moves the objects in the arc between the new node and its predecessor, and removing a node only moves that node's objects to its successor. Finding the successor is a binary search over the sorted node positions, which makes lookups `O(log n)`.

title: Cache the small values that dominate real usage
takeaway: Preallocating a skewed-hot range of values trades a little startup work for many avoided allocations.
section: Verifying if these integers are indeed referenced often

blocks.text: Python preallocates integers from -5 to 256 at interpreter start and reuses those singletons instead of allocating a new object for each occurrence. Reference counts confirm the skew: 0 is referenced 359 times during startup while counts fall as values grow, and the scheme saves about 1993 allocations. The optimization works because small values are accessed far more often than large ones, so a fixed cache covers most requests.

title: Equal values are not always the same object
takeaway: Identity can coincide with equality for cached values and diverge for everything else.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: `id()` returns an object's memory address, and for integers in -5 to 256 two equal values return the same address because both refer to the preallocated singleton. For larger values, equal numbers live at different addresses. Any reasoning that treats object identity as a proxy for numeric equality therefore holds only inside the cached range.

title: Precompute the answer for every element when the same query repeats
takeaway: Spending space on precomputed positions collapses many searches into one.

blocks.text: If every element stores a k-item position tuple giving its index in each of k sorted lists, a query needs only one binary search over a merged list of all `k * n` elements. The matching element's tuple supplies the position in every list at once, reducing `O(k log n)` to `O(log(kn))`. The cost is `O(k * kn)` space, since each of the `k * n` elements carries k integers.

title: Bridge each sorted list to the next so the search narrows as it descends
takeaway: Carrying a position across levels replaces repeated binary searches with constant-time checks.

blocks.text: Fractional cascading builds auxiliary lists that mix each original list with every other element of the list below, and each element stores a bridge to its position in that lower list. One binary search on the top list plus a check of the bridged index and the index before it is enough at each lower level, because the promoted elements guarantee the target cannot lie further away. The result is `O(k + log n)` time with `O(kn)` space, since the auxiliary lists total less than twice the original data.

reference.title: Fractional Cascading - Original Paper by Bernard Chazelle and Leonidas Guibas

title: Share by reference and copy only when the first write arrives
takeaway: Deferring the copy makes read-heavy sharing nearly free and read-only copies free entirely.

blocks.text: Copy-on-write gives both instances a reference to the same resource and clones it just before the first modification, so access and traversal cost nothing extra. `fork` uses this: the child starts as a reference to the parent's program space and copies only the pages it writes, which keeps process creation fast. In the fork-exec pattern the child replaces its program immediately and never writes, so the deep copy never happens at all.

title: Copy only the path from the changed node to the root
takeaway: Structural sharing narrows a copy to the nodes an update actually touches.

blocks.text: Instead of cloning an entire tree, a copy-on-write update clones the modified node and its ancestors up to the root, while every untouched subtree stays shared between the old and new versions. A change deep in a tree therefore costs `O(log n)` new nodes rather than `O(n)`, and both versions remain valid simultaneously. This path-copying scheme is the basis of persistent data structures, which keep every past version accessible.

title: A full table scan can evict the entire working set from an LRU cache
takeaway: A scan larger than the cache turns a good hit ratio into a cold cache.

blocks.text: Strict LRU inserts every newly read page at the head, so scanning a table bigger than the buffer pool pushes out the pages the workload actually depends on. If the scanned pages are never read again, the eviction buys nothing and the hit ratio collapses until normal traffic refills the cache. The damage scales with table size, not with how often the scan runs.

reference.title: Least Recently Used cache eviction strategy

title: Insert new pages at the midpoint so one-touch pages leave first
takeaway: Separating first-touch pages from proven-hot pages keeps scans from displacing the working set.

blocks.text: InnoDB splits the buffer pool into a young sublist of 5/8 and an old sublist of 3/8, inserts new pages at the head of the old sublist rather than at the top of the cache, and evicts from the tail of the old sublist. A page touched a second time is promoted to the head of the young sublist and stays longer, while a page read once by a scan ages out quickly. The split is tunable through `innodb_old_blocks_pct`, whose default of 37 corresponds to the 3/8 old portion.

reference.title: MySQL Dev - Making the Buffer Pool Scan Resistant

title: Model each state as a coroutine paused on its next input
takeaway: States become readable, resumable units instead of flags scattered across one loop.

blocks.text: A state is an infinite loop that waits at `yield` for the next token, decides the transition, and updates the machine's current state. The paused function keeps its own frame, so no thread runs between inputs and control returns to the caller. An FSM class holds the states and exposes a `send` method that forwards each input to whichever state is current.

title: Keep each transition next to the state that owns it
takeaway: Local transition logic keeps the state diagram and the code from drifting apart.

blocks.text: Rather than one growing `if`/`elif` ladder covering every state, each state's coroutine contains only its outgoing edges and mutates the shared `current_state`. The dispatcher shrinks to a single forward: receive the input, hand it to the current state. Because each edge in the diagram maps to one branch in one function, adding a state does not require touching unrelated code.

title: Shrink a sparse average toward the system mean
takeaway: A prior stops a handful of ratings from vaulting an item to the top.

blocks.text: Bayesian average blends an item's mean `A` with the system mean `S`, weighted by how many ratings `m` the item has against the average `m_avg`. With few ratings the score sits near `S`, and as `m` grows the weight shifts to `A`. On a MovieLens ranking, the plain arithmetic mean put ten movies with a single 5-out-of-5 rating at the top, while the shrunk score surfaced broadly rated films.

title: A sum of ratings ranks popularity, not quality, and never bounds
takeaway: Cumulative scores let volume beat merit and produce numbers no ranking can normalize.

blocks.text: Scoring by total rating points gives an item with 10,000 one-star ratings a score of 10,000 and an item with 1,000 five-star ratings a score of 5,000, so the worse item wins. The score also grows without limit, which makes thresholds and cross-category comparisons unstable. A bounded mean-like score avoids both problems.

reference.title: How not to sort by Average Rating

title: Sub-aggregate counters coarsely to cap the work per request
takeaway: The cost of a sliding window is the number of buckets scanned, not the window's length.

blocks.text: Keeping one counter per second means an hour-long window requires summing 3,600 entries on every request. Store counts per minute instead and the same window needs about 60 sums, with the window sliding per minute. Persisting the granularity in configuration makes the tradeoff between precision and cost explicit.

title: Split limiter state into durable config and hot counters
takeaway: Configuration and request counts have opposite access patterns and belong in different stores.

blocks.text: Configuration changes rarely but must survive machine failure, so it belongs in a disk-backed key-value store keyed by user, IP, or token. Request counts change on every call and are read and written constantly, so they belong in memory close to the decision engine. Putting both in one SQL table bottlenecks the path that runs on every request.

title: A term is informative because it is rare, not because it repeats
takeaway: Weighting by document frequency is what turns word counts into a relevance signal.

blocks.text: Inverse document frequency falls as a term appears in more documents, so `a`, `and`, and `the` get near-zero weight while a distinctive term scores high. Multiplying term frequency by IDF boosts documents that use a rare query term often and suppresses matches on filler words. The measure was introduced as term specificity, reflecting that rarity is the property being rewarded.

reference.title: A statistical interpretation of term specificity and its application in retrieval

title: Choose an IDF variant by its behavior at the boundaries
takeaway: The formula's edge cases decide whether a TF-IDF score collapses to zero or goes negative.

blocks.text: The common IDF hits 0 when a term appears in every document and is undefined at zero documents, either of which can erase a score when multiplied by term frequency. Smooth IDF avoids both endpoints at the cost of never reaching zero. Probabilistic IDF goes negative once a term appears in more than half the documents, which is useful when such terms should be actively penalized.

reference.title: Understanding Inverse Document Frequency: On theoretical arguments for IDF

title: Read expert code until the unfamiliar becomes familiar
takeaway: Skimming real codebases builds vocabulary faster than writing another toy program.

blocks.text: Pick an open-source project and skim it even when little makes sense at first. After a few passes the structure and business logic start to click because the same names and patterns recur. Repeated exposure to how experts organize code expands the set of designs you can recognize and reuse.

title: Learn the paradigm, not just the language that expresses it
takeaway: Constructs transfer across languages; syntax does not.

blocks.text: A language is a tool for expressing business logic, and the durable knowledge lives in its constructs: functional programming, polymorphism, event-driven design, the actor model. Once a construct is understood, it can be carried into another language, such as using JavaScript-style callbacks in Python to build generic action functions. Learning only syntax ties the skill to one runtime.

title: Assign a stateful object to a prompt and Python stringifies it each time
takeaway: The prompt can display live state if rendering is deferred to an object.

blocks.text: When `sys.ps1` holds a non-string, Python calls `str()` on that object every time a prompt is displayed. A class that increments a counter inside `__str__` therefore renders a fresh line number on each prompt, the way IPython numbers statements. The same hook can show branch, environment, or elapsed time without a background thread.

title: Run shell setup from PYTHONSTARTUP before the first prompt
takeaway: Interactive-only configuration belongs in a startup file, not retyped every session.
section: Setting new prompt strings every time the shell starts

blocks.text: `PYTHONSTARTUP` names a readable file that the interactive interpreter executes before showing the first prompt. Put prompt styling and helper imports there, and every new shell starts configured. The file runs only in interactive mode, so scripts and production runs are unaffected.

title: A three-cell rule can generate aperiodic, unpredictable output
takeaway: Local determinism does not imply global regularity, which is exactly what a PRNG needs.

blocks.text: Rule 30 sets each cell from itself and its two neighbors using `left XOR (central OR right)`. Starting from a single black cell, the grid produces large triangles but no recognizable overall pattern, and its center column passes standard randomness tests. Mathematica used that column to generate random integers.

title: Use the seed as an offset into a deterministic stream
takeaway: Skipping into the sequence hides the predictable start without changing the generator.

blocks.text: Reading the center column from row 0 yields the same numbers on every run, so the generator must enter the stream somewhere else. Take a seed such as the current timestamp, skip that many bits, then read batches of `n` bits to form each number. Using the seed as the initial row is faster but makes output quality depend heavily on the seed.

title: Python keeps one entry per name, so dispatch needs a signature registry
takeaway: Overloading is impossible in the namespace but easy in a dictionary keyed by signature.

blocks.text: Defining a second function with the same name overwrites the first entry returned by `locals()`, leaving only one implementation visible. A decorator can register each definition in a singleton namespace under a key of module, class, name, and argument count. Calls then look up the matching key and invoke the stored implementation.

title: Disambiguate overloads on the cheapest signature dimension
takeaway: Argument count resolves most overloads without inspecting types on every call.

blocks.text: Counting arguments is enough to separate a one-argument circle area from a two-argument rectangle area, and the count is available from the call itself. Types can be added as a second dimension when overloads share an arity, at the cost of a more expensive lookup. What can be inspected is bounded by `getfullargspec`.

title: Isolate anomalies with random splits instead of modeling normal
takeaway: Scoring by how quickly a point separates avoids the false positives of profile-the-normal methods.

blocks.text: Random decision trees split on a random attribute at a random value, and anomalous points, being few and different, reach a leaf in fewer splits. The average path length across a forest becomes the anomaly score, so no distance or density calculation is needed. Methods built to characterize normal points instead spend their capacity there and mislabel the edges.

title: Sub-sampling separates anomalies better than using all the data
takeaway: More data can blur the boundary, while a random subset makes anomalies stand out.

blocks.text: In a full dataset, normal points can sit close enough to anomalies to mask them, producing false negatives. Building each tree from a random sub-sample thins that crowd and makes the separation visible. This runs opposite to most learning methods, which assume more data always improves accuracy.

title: Hide the existence of a message, not only its meaning
takeaway: Encryption protects content but still advertises that something was sent; concealment protects the act.

blocks.text: Cryptography makes an intercepted message unreadable, yet the interception itself reveals that communication is taking place. Steganography embeds the payload in an ordinary carrier so an observer does not know a message exists at all. Layering the two, by encrypting first and hiding the result, covers both the content and the fact of transmission.

title: An index is not a value, so a one-bit edit can change everything
takeaway: LSB substitution only stays invisible when the stored number maps monotonically to appearance.

blocks.text: In a palette image each pixel is a one-byte index into a color table, not a color intensity. Flipping the low bit moves the pixel to a neighboring table entry, which may hold an unrelated color and become immediately visible. Sorting the palette by color or adding near-duplicate entries makes adjacent indices look alike and restores the assumption that a small numeric change is also a small visual one.

title: Insert the payload between the lossy and lossless stages
takeaway: A pipeline that destroys data in one step and preserves it in the next gives you a safe insertion point.

blocks.text: JPEG first removes redundancy through DCT and quantization, then encodes the result losslessly with Huffman coding. Data embedded before quantization would be lost, destroyed, or visibly altered by that step, while data inserted after it passes through the lossless stage untouched. Sandwiching the payload in that gap lets steganography survive the file format's own compression.

title: Arbitrary precision is a variable-length array, not a wider register
takeaway: Once the digit count is stored beside the digits, the only remaining limit is memory.

blocks.text: CPython's integer struct carries an `ob_size` count and a pointer to a `digit` array, the same variable-length shape used by tuples and lists. Reallocating that array lets a value grow past 64 bits instead of overflowing. Since Python 3 every integer is a bignum, bounded by host memory rather than by a fixed machine word.

title: Pack a full machine word per digit instead of one decimal place
takeaway: Choosing a radix near the word size multiplies storage efficiency without complicating arithmetic.

blocks.text: Storing one decimal digit in a 32-bit slot leaves 28 bits unused, because the value only ranges from 0 to 9. CPython instead converts numbers to base 2^30, so each digit spans 0 to 1,073,741,823 and the array uses almost every allocated bit. Addition and subtraction still operate digit by digit with carry, exactly like grade-school arithmetic.

title: A primitive you patch is also part of the boot sequence
takeaway: Changing a core operation globally breaks the code that initializes the runtime before your test ever runs.

blocks.text: Replacing `BINARY_ADD` with a random choice among five operators made the interpreter segfault during build and initialization, because startup code performs additions too. The randomized path had to be gated by a flag set only when execution came from the interactive shell, leaving every other caller with normal addition. An experiment on a primitive must be scoped by entry point rather than applied globally.

title: Asymptotic costs stay hidden until the result set is large enough
takeaway: A single-scale benchmark can rank two approaches backwards; measure at several sizes and find the crossover.

blocks.text: Below about 500 to 600 documents, `skip` plus `limit` and `_id` plus `limit` had comparable response times. Past that threshold the skip approach rose sharply while the `_id` approach stayed nearly constant regardless of result-set size. Benchmarking only a small page would have missed the divergence entirely.

title: Skipping rows costs work proportional to the offset
takeaway: `skip` must walk every discarded document, so deep pages get slower no matter how well the collection is indexed.

blocks.text: MongoDB's `skip(n)` advances the cursor by iterating over and discarding `n` documents instead of jumping to a position. The call does not use an index, so adding one does not improve skipping speed. The cost is negligible for a small result set, which is why `skip` remains a reasonable choice near the first few pages.

title: Page by seeking past the last key, not by counting offsets
takeaway: A range query on an indexed sort key keeps page cost flat as the collection grows.

blocks.text: Fetch a page, remember the last document's `_id`, then ask for documents greater than that id with a limit. ObjectIds are naturally ordered and `_id` is always indexed, so each page becomes a short index range instead of a count of rows to discard. The cursor is a value in the data, which is what makes keyset pagination independent of how deep the page is.

title: An HTTP request is plain text you can type into a TCP socket
takeaway: Seeing the request line and headers as raw bytes demystifies what every client library does.

blocks.text: HTTP runs over a TCP connection, and a request is a method, path, version, headers, and optional body written as text. Netcat opens the connection and forwards standard input, so typing a valid request by hand returns the same response a browser gets. Sending bytes that are not a valid request earns a 400, showing that the server parses the message rather than trusting a client.

title: A stable procedure can live in the weights instead of the prompt
takeaway: For a repeated, well-defined workflow, a compiled adapter can match a frontier model at a fraction of the token cost.

blocks.text: A 3,500-token incident-triage SOP was compiled into a QLoRA-tuned 3B model instead of being resent on every turn. The compiled model reached 93.0% end-to-end accuracy against Gemini 2.5 Pro's 92.0%, while cutting input tokens from 5,200 to 450 per incident and cost from $1.85 to $0.22 per 1,000 incidents. The prompt kept only a trigger token; the state machine lived in the adapter. This works when the procedure is stable and high-volume, not when the rules change every week.

title: Mask the loss on tool outputs so the model learns decisions, not telemetry
takeaway: In multi-turn tool-calling traces, only the assistant's actions deserve gradient.
section: The Training Setup: Loss Masking On Assistant Turns

blocks.text: Most tokens in a tool-calling trace are user alerts, system triggers and tool responses. Computing loss over all of them teaches the model to predict random telemetry numbers and commit hashes instead of the next decision. Label those tokens `-100` so gradients flow only through the assistant's actions, and the adapter learns the procedure rather than the simulator's noise.

title: Slop debt is incoherence, not technical debt at volume
takeaway: The danger of generated code is not how much there is; it is that nobody chose its shape.
section: Why It Is Not The Same Thing

blocks.text: Classic tech debt comes from a decision: you skipped an abstraction or hardcoded a value to ship sooner, and the reason can be recovered later. Slop debt comes from the absence of a decision: the model chose variable names, error handling and layers independently for every file, with no memory of the last one. The result compiles and passes tests, but two functions that look identical may solve the same problem in different ways because no architect enforced consistency.

title: Slop debt compounds because the model reads its own output
takeaway: Every generation pass turns existing incoherence into context for the next pass.

blocks.text: Once a codebase contains hundreds of files of locally correct but globally inconsistent code, the next generation pass uses that code as context. It copies the bad abstraction because that is what it sees, and adds a third error-handling style because it cannot tell which of the first two is intended. Each cycle does not just add debt; it teaches the next cycle to add debt faster, in the same shape. A human eventually gets frustrated and refactors, but a model has no opinion about whether the pattern is good.

title: AI moves the bottleneck from writing code to verifying it
takeaway: If your process still optimizes for typing speed, it is optimizing for a constraint that no longer exists.

blocks.text: Every engineering process was built to manage scarce implementation time. Agentic coding removes typing as the bottleneck, but verification, review and security take its place. The constraint moves rather than disappearing, so the useful question is which ritual still closes a gap and which one only survives out of habit.

title: Ask the model before the person
takeaway: The model watched the change; the author may no longer be the fastest path to context.
section: Ask The Model Before The Person

blocks.text: Before agentic coding, “who wrote this” was the fastest way to get context because the author held knowledge nobody else had. Now the model can walk the git history, summarize ownership from CODEOWNERS and recent commits, and pull the PR discussion. Ask what you actually need to know, then reserve the human for judgment calls the model cannot make, and automate any category of question you ask repeatedly.

title: Docs rot silently; tools fail loudly
takeaway: Encode operational knowledge as executable tools, not prose nobody notices is stale.
section: Why Build Tools Instead of Writing Docs

blocks.text: A stale wiki page can mislead people for months because nothing forces it to reveal that it is wrong. A broken tool fails in front of the next person who uses it, so it actually gets fixed. That difference matters more now that AI agents act on the same instructions: an agent reading a stale runbook has no reliable way to know it is stale, while an agent calling a broken tool gets an immediate failure.

title: Build the debugging skill before the other two
takeaway: Incidents happen on their own schedule, so every one can add a verified failure pattern.

blocks.text: The debugging skill should match live symptoms to known failure patterns for that service, link directly to the relevant logs, traces and dashboards, and run diagnostics instead of pointing at raw data. Start with the service that pages most and takes longest to fix, because that is where the payoff is visible immediately. Each incident then becomes a chance to add a verified pattern rather than another manual investigation.

title: Never let the judge come from the same model family
takeaway: LLM judges systematically favor their own family's text, so an independent judge is required.
section: The Bias You Need to Know About

blocks.text: LLM judges show a measurable self-preference bias: they favor text generated by models from their own family, even when human reviewers prefer the alternative. A judge that shares a family with the system under test will therefore over-score it. Use a different family for the judge, pin its version, and calibrate the rubric against human-labeled examples before trusting the scores.

title: A precise rubric turns an LLM judge from a vibe check into a procedure
takeaway: G-Eval's consistency comes from defining the dimension precisely and making the judge write its evaluation steps before scoring.

blocks.text: A vague 1–5 rubric gives the judge no anchor, so it falls back on “does this look fine” and cannot separate a mediocre output from a strong one. G-Eval defines the criterion in concrete terms, has the model generate evaluation steps from that definition, and then scores examples with the steps in view. The generated steps also leave an audit trail: when a score looks wrong, you can see where the judge's reasoning diverged.

title: Topological sort turns a dependency graph into a schedule
takeaway: Model the workflow as a DAG first; the execution order and the parallelism then fall out of the graph.

blocks.text: A workflow is a set of tasks that produce and consume outputs, and a consumer cannot run before its producer finishes. A directed acyclic graph represents those dependencies; a topological order lists every node after the nodes it depends on. Nodes at the same level have no dependency between them, so they can run concurrently. That is what lets an orchestrator dispatch parallel branches without hardcoding the sequence.

title: Topological sort gives order, not load balance
takeaway: A correct schedule can still have a critical path that leaves most of the cluster waiting.

blocks.text: If ten parallel tasks all feed into one merge node, the merge cannot start until the slowest of the ten finishes. Topological sort orders the work correctly but does not make the fan-in smaller or move work off the critical path. Profile the longest chain of dependent tasks and the largest fan-in node; that is where parallelism actually pays off.
